65465.e: In the scriptorium, monks copied books by hand. The word comes from the Latin “scribere”, to write.
65465.m: In the scriptorium, monks copied books.

65466.e: Parchment is made from the skins of calves, sheep or goats. The skin is cleaned, stretched and scraped thin.
65466.m: Parchment is made from animal skin.

65467.q: What did monks in the Middle Ages usually write with?
65467.e: The monks cut quills, usually from geese, at an angle and dipped them in ink.
65467.m: Monks wrote with cut bird feathers.

65468.q: What is a large, artistically decorated first letter in a manuscript called?
65468.e: An initial stands at the beginning of a chapter. It is often painted in colour and decorated with gold, tendrils or figures.
65468.m: A decorated first letter is called an initial.

65469.q: What is the art of decorating manuscripts with colourful pictures called?
65469.e: In manuscript illumination, pictures and ornaments were painted directly into the manuscript. It is also called illumination.

65470.q: Which script from the time of Charlemagne is the basis of our lower-case letters?
65470.e: Carolingian minuscule was easy to read and spread throughout the Frankish kingdom. Our lower-case letters of today developed from it.
65470.m: Our lower-case letters come from Carolingian minuscule.

65471.q: In which Swiss city is the famous abbey library with ancient manuscripts from monasteries?
65471.e: The Abbey Library of St Gallen is one of the oldest libraries in the world. It holds manuscripts written by monks over 1000 years ago.
65471.m: The famous abbey library is in St Gallen.

65472.q: Why did people in the Middle Ages sometimes scrape old writing off parchment?
a: Because parchment was expensive and they wanted to reuse it
Because they wanted to eat the parchment
65472.e: Parchment was precious. So old texts were scraped off and new ones written on top. Such a page is called a palimpsest.
65472.m: Expensive parchment was scraped and written on again.

65473.q: In which year did the East-West Schism between the Eastern and Western Churches take place?
65473.e: In 1054 the representatives of Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other. This event is seen as the beginning of the split in the Church.
65473.m: The Church split into East and West in 1054.

65474.q: Which church formed in the East after the schism?
65474.e: The Eastern Church calls itself Orthodox, which means “of the right belief”. The Western Church became the Roman Catholic Church.
65474.m: The Orthodox Church formed in the East.

65475.q: Which city was the centre of the Eastern Church in 1054?
65475.e: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, was the capital of the Byzantine Empire and the seat of the Patriarch.
65475.m: Constantinople was the centre of the Eastern Church.

65476.q: Which two cities faced each other in the schism of 1054?
65476.e: In 1054, the Pope's envoys from Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. Rome became the centre of the Western Church, Constantinople the centre of the Eastern Church.

65477.q: In which church did the papal envoys place the bull of excommunication on the altar in 1054?
65477.e: Cardinal Humbert placed the document of excommunication on the altar of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. It was the main church of the Byzantine Empire.
65477.m: In 1054 the bull of excommunication lay on the altar of the Hagia Sophia.

65478.q: What, among other things, did the Eastern and Western Churches argue about before the schism?
a: The building of St Peter's Basilica
65478.e: The Pope in Rome wanted to decide for the whole Church. The Eastern Church saw him only as first among equals. There was also a dispute about a phrase in the creed.
65478.m: East and West argued about the power of the Pope.

65479.q: What does the Greek word “schism” mean?
65479.e: “Schism” comes from the Greek word for a split or tear. It means a division of the Church.
65479.m: A schism is a split in the Church.

65480.q: Who called for the First Crusade in 1095?
65480.e: In 1095, in a speech in France, Pope Urban II called for a crusade to Jerusalem.
65480.m: The Pope called for the crusade in 1095.

65481.q: Which city did the crusaders mainly want to conquer?
65481.e: The goal was Jerusalem with the tomb of Jesus. The city was under Muslim rule.
65481.m: The crusaders wanted to conquer Jerusalem.

65482.q: Which Muslim ruler recaptured Jerusalem in 1187?
65482.e: Saladin, Sultan of Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusaders at Hattin and took Jerusalem. This triggered the Third Crusade.

65483.q: Which English king took part in the Third Crusade?
65483.e: Richard I of England, known as the Lionheart, fought against Saladin. But he did not recapture Jerusalem.
65483.m: Richard the Lionheart fought in the Third Crusade.

65484.q: Which Christian city did the crusaders conquer and plunder in 1204 in the Fourth Crusade?
65484.e: Instead of going to the Holy Land, the crusaders attacked Constantinople. The plundering deepened the rift between the Eastern and Western Churches.
65484.m: The Fourth Crusade ended with the plundering of Constantinople.

65485.q: How did Emperor Frederick Barbarossa die on the Third Crusade in 1190?
65485.e: Barbarossa drowned in the River Saleph in the south of present-day Turkey. Many of his soldiers then went home.
65485.m: Barbarossa drowned on the crusade in 1190.

65486.q: Which order of knights was founded in Jerusalem at the time of the Crusades?
65486.e: The Templars were founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims in the Holy Land. They were monks and knights at the same time.
65486.m: The Knights Templar were founded at the time of the Crusades.

65487.q: Which shape of arch is typical of Romanesque churches?
65487.e: Romanesque windows, doorways and arcades have semicircular round arches.
65487.m: Romanesque churches can be recognised by their round arches.

65488.q: What do the walls and windows of Romanesque churches usually look like?
65488.e: The heavy vaults needed thick walls. Large windows would have weakened the walls, which is why Romanesque churches are rather dark inside.
65488.m: Romanesque churches have thick walls and small windows.

65489.q: When was the Romanesque style mainly used for building in Europe?
65489.e: The Romanesque period lasted roughly from 1000 to 1250. After that, Gothic took over.
65489.m: Romanesque was the building style of about 1000 to 1250.

65490.e: From about 1150 to 1250, Gothic took over. It has pointed arches, tall spaces and large windows.

65491.q: Which Zurich church is a well-known Romanesque building?
65491.e: The Grossmünster was built in the Romanesque style from about 1100 to 1220. Its twin towers are a landmark of Zurich.
65491.m: The Grossmünster in Zurich is Romanesque.

65492.q: What is the semicircular end of the church interior, often behind the altar, called?
65492.e: The apse is a semicircular recess at the end of the choir. In Romanesque churches it was often decorated with paintings.
65492.m: The apse is the semicircular end of a church.

65493.q: What is the vault that looks like a pipe cut in half, common in Romanesque buildings, called?
65493.e: A barrel vault has a semicircular cross-section like half a barrel. Fan, net and star vaults belong to the Gothic period.
65493.m: The barrel vault is typical of Romanesque architecture.

65494.q: Why is this architectural style called “Romanesque”?
a: It was invented by the Romansh
It is named after a master builder called Roman
65494.e: The name was coined in the 19th century. Round arches and massive walls recalled the architecture of the ancient Romans.
65494.m: Romanesque is named after its Roman models.

65495.q: Which shape of arch is typical of Gothic cathedrals?
65495.e: The pointed arch directs the weight downwards more steeply. This allowed taller spaces to be built.
65495.m: Gothic churches can be recognised by their pointed arches.

65496.q: What is the system of supports on the outside of Gothic churches that takes the load off the walls called?
65496.e: Buttresses and flying buttresses take the pressure of the vaults on the outside. That is why the walls could be thin and have large windows.
65496.m: Flying buttresses support Gothic churches from the outside.

65497.q: What is the large round window with tracery on many Gothic cathedrals called?
65497.e: The rose window is a large round window like a flower. Notre-Dame de Paris, for example, has famous rose windows.
65497.m: A round Gothic flower-like window is called a rose window.

65498.q: What did Gothic builders want to bring into the church with large windows?
65498.e: Around 1140, Abbot Suger had the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris built with large windows. Light was seen as a sign of God.
65498.m: Gothic churches were meant to be bright and full of light.

65499.q: In which country did Gothic architecture begin?
65499.e: Gothic architecture began in the 12th century in the area around Paris. From there it spread across the whole of Europe.

65500.q: In which city on the Rhine is the famous Gothic cathedral with two tall towers?
65500.e: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 and only completed in 1880. It is one of the largest Gothic churches in the world.
65500.m: Cologne Cathedral is a famous Gothic cathedral.

65501.q: What are the figures, often shaped like mythical creatures, that carry rainwater off the roof of a Gothic church called?
65501.e: Gargoyles carry rainwater far away from the walls. They are often shaped like dragons, demons or animals.
65501.m: Gargoyles protect Gothic walls from rainwater.

65502.q: In which year did the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris burn?
65502.e: On 15 April 2019, a fire destroyed the roof and the spire. After rebuilding, the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

65503.q: Which Gothic minster has the tallest church tower in Germany, at about 161 metres?
65503.e: The tower of Ulm Minster is about 161.5 metres high and was completed in 1890. For a long time it was the tallest church tower in the world, until the Sagrada Família in Barcelona overtook it in October 2025.
65503.m: Ulm Minster has the tallest church tower in Germany.

65504.q: Which city does the Way of St James lead to?
65504.e: All the Ways of St James end in Santiago de Compostela. The cathedral with the apostle's tomb is there.
65504.m: The Way of St James leads to Santiago de Compostela.

65505.q: Whose tomb do pilgrims visit on the Way of St James?
65505.e: According to tradition, James the Great, a disciple of Jesus, is buried in Santiago.
65505.m: Pilgrims visit the tomb of James in Santiago.

65506.q: Which sign do pilgrims on the Way of St James often wear on their rucksack?
65506.e: The scallop shell is the symbol of the Way of St James. It also shows the direction on many signposts.
65506.m: The scallop shell is the pilgrims' sign.

65507.q: What do pilgrims on the Way of St James collect in their pilgrim passport?
65507.e: In the pilgrim passport, the credencial, pilgrims collect stamps from hostels and churches. This proves the route they have taken.
65507.m: Pilgrims collect stamps in their pilgrim passport.

65508.q: How many kilometres must you walk at least to receive the pilgrim certificate in Santiago?
65508.e: Anyone who walks the last 100 kilometres receives the certificate called the “Compostela”. By bike it is 200 kilometres.
65508.m: For the pilgrim certificate you must walk at least 100 kilometres.

65509.q: In which country is Santiago de Compostela, the goal of the Way of St James?
65509.e: Santiago de Compostela is in Galicia in north-west Spain. All the Ways of St James end there.
65509.m: The Way of St James ends in Spain.

65510.e: From 1209, Francis of Assisi gathered brothers around him who lived in poverty and preached.
65510.m: Francis of Assisi founded the Franciscans.

65511.q: What kind of order are the Franciscans?
65511.e: The brothers owned nothing and lived from work and donations. That is why they are called a mendicant (begging) order.
65511.m: The Franciscans are a mendicant order.

65512.q: What is the famous song in which Francis praises the sun, moon and water as brothers and sisters?
65512.e: In the Canticle of the Sun, Francis praises God for “Brother Sun” and “Sister Moon”. It is regarded as one of the first poems in the Italian language.
65512.m: Francis of Assisi wrote the Canticle of the Sun.

65513.q: What colour is the Franciscans' habit usually?
65513.e: Franciscans usually wear a brown habit with a rope as a belt. The knots in the rope are a reminder of their vows.

65514.q: What are the nuns named after Clare of Assisi called?
65514.e: Clare of Assisi followed Francis and founded the women's branch. Her sisters are called Poor Clares.
65514.m: The Poor Clares are the sisters of the Franciscans.

65516.q: Which order arose in the 16th century as a reform branch of the Franciscans and is widespread in Switzerland?
65516.e: The Capuchins were confirmed by the Pope in 1528. They get their name from the pointed hood (cappuccio) of their habit.
65516.m: The Capuchins belong to the Franciscan family.

65517.q: Which order did Hildegard of Bingen belong to?
65517.e: Hildegard lived by the Rule of St Benedict. She became abbess of a community of women.
65517.m: Hildegard of Bingen was a Benedictine nun.

65519.q: For which field of knowledge is Hildegard especially well known today?
65519.e: Hildegard wrote about plants, animals, stones and illnesses. Her books on medicine are still read today.
65519.m: Hildegard wrote about nature and medicine.

65520.q: Apart from writing and healing, what else did Hildegard do?
65520.e: Hildegard wrote many sacred songs and the musical play “Ordo Virtutum”. Her music is still sung today.

65521.q: According to her own words, what had Hildegard experienced since childhood?
65521.e: In her own words, Hildegard had seen images and lights since childhood, which she understood as messages from God. She wrote these visions down in the book “Scivias”.
65521.m: Hildegard had visions and wrote them down.

65522.q: Which special title did Pope Benedict XVI give Hildegard in 2012?
65522.e: In 2012 Hildegard was declared a saint and made a Doctor of the Church. Only a few women hold this title.
65522.m: Hildegard has been a Doctor of the Church since 2012.

65523.q: What did Hildegard invent with the “Lingua ignota”?
65523.e: The “Lingua ignota”, the “unknown language”, had its own words and letters. Its purpose is still not entirely clear today.

65524.q: On which river is the town of Bingen?
65524.e: Bingen lies where the River Nahe flows into the Rhine. Hildegard's convents were nearby.

65525.q: What does the Latin word “inquisitio” mean?
65525.e: “Inquisitio” comes from “inquirere”, to inquire. The Inquisition investigated whether someone departed from Church teaching.

65526.q: In the Middle Ages, what were people called who departed from official Church teaching?
65526.e: Heretics held teachings that the Church considered wrong. The Inquisition persecuted them.
65526.m: People who departed from the faith were called heretics.

65527.q: Which religious group in southern France was persecuted especially harshly in the 13th century?
65527.e: The Cathars, also called Albigensians, rejected the rich Church. There was even a crusade against them and later the Inquisition.
65527.m: The Cathars were persecuted in southern France.

65528.q: Which mendicant order provided especially many inquisitors in the Middle Ages?
65528.e: The popes often gave the Inquisition to the Dominicans, because they were well trained in theology.

65529.q: In which period did the Church's Inquisition begin?
a: In the time of the pharaohs
65529.e: From about 1231, the popes appointed their own judges to prosecute heretics. That was in the Middle Ages.
65529.m: The Inquisition began in the Middle Ages.

65530.q: In which country was the Inquisition especially feared from 1478?
65530.e: The Spanish Inquisition was founded in 1478. It persecuted many people and passed harsh sentences.
65530.m: The Spanish Inquisition was especially feared.

65531.q: Where were the sentences of the Spanish Inquisition often announced?
a: In public in a large square
65531.e: The sentences were solemnly announced in a square in front of many spectators. This was called an auto-da-fé, an act of faith.
65531.m: The Inquisition announced its sentences in public.

65532.q: Who carried out death sentences passed after an Inquisition trial?
65532.e: The Church handed condemned people over to the “secular arm”, meaning princes and towns. These carried out the punishments.
65532.m: The secular authorities carried out the punishments.

65533.q: In the late Middle Ages, what did the Church promise when someone bought a letter of indulgence?
65533.e: An indulgence was supposed to shorten or cancel temporal punishment for sins, for example in purgatory. Many people paid money for it.
65533.m: An indulgence was supposed to shorten punishment for sins.

65534.q: Which Dominican monk travelled through Germany around 1517 as a well-known preacher of indulgences?
65534.e: Johann Tetzel preached for the indulgence on behalf of the Archbishop of Mainz. His sermons made Martin Luther very angry.
65534.m: Johann Tetzel was the most famous preacher of indulgences.

65535.q: For which building in Rome was money collected with the indulgence of 1517?
65535.e: Part of the money from the indulgence went into rebuilding St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Another part went to Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg.
65535.m: The indulgence of 1517 helped to build St Peter's Basilica.

65536.q: Which saying is linked to the sale of indulgences around Tetzel?
a: As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs
Pray and work, and all will be well
No pain, no gain in heaven
65536.e: The saying sums up how indulgences were sold: money in exchange for shorter punishment in purgatory. It is still well known today.
65536.m: The coffer saying shows how indulgences were sold for money.

65537.q: Who profited from the great sale of indulgences in 1517?
65537.e: Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg received half the income to pay off his debts. The rest went to the Pope for building St Peter's Basilica.
65537.m: An archbishop and the Pope profited from the indulgence.

65538.q: Who was at the head of the Catholic Church when Luther protested against indulgences?
65538.e: At that time Leo X from the Medici family was Pope. He announced the indulgence for building St Peter's Basilica.
65538.m: The Pope in Rome had the indulgence sold.

65539.q: Which reformer preached against the sale of indulgences in Switzerland?
65539.e: From 1518 the monk Bernhardin Samson sold indulgences in the Swiss Confederation. Zwingli preached against it, and in 1519 Samson was called back to Rome.
65539.m: Zwingli criticised the sale of indulgences in Switzerland.

65540.q: In which year did Martin Luther publish his 95 Theses?
65540.e: On 31 October 1517, Luther sent his theses against indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz. This date is seen as the start of the Reformation.
65540.m: The Reformation began in 1517 with Luther's theses.

65541.q: On which date is Reformation Day celebrated today?
65541.e: Reformation Day recalls the day on which Luther made his theses known. Many Reformed churches celebrate Reformation Sunday on the first Sunday in November.

65542.q: In which town is Luther said to have nailed the theses to the door of the Castle Church?
65542.e: Luther was a professor at the University of Wittenberg. Whether he really nailed the theses to the door of the Castle Church is disputed among historians.
65542.m: Wittenberg is the town of the 95 Theses.

65543.q: In which language did Luther originally write the 95 Theses?
65543.e: The theses were intended for a scholarly debate and were therefore written in Latin. They were soon translated into German and widely spread.
65543.m: The 95 Theses were first in Latin.

65544.q: What was the main subject of Luther's 95 Theses?
65544.e: Luther criticised the idea that you could buy yourself free from punishment for sins with money. True repentance comes from the heart.
65544.m: Luther's theses were directed against indulgences.

65545.q: What was Martin Luther's job before he became a reformer?
65545.e: Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483. He entered a monastery and later became a professor of theology in Wittenberg.
65545.m: Luther was a monk and professor in Wittenberg.

65546.q: Before which emperor did Luther have to answer in Worms in 1521?
65546.e: Emperor Charles V led the Diet of Worms in 1521. Luther was supposed to retract his writings there.
65546.m: In Worms, Luther stood before Emperor Charles V.

65547.q: What was demanded of Luther in Worms?
a: He was to retract his writings
He was to become a bishop
He was to translate the Bible
He was to make a pilgrimage to Rome
65547.e: Luther was supposed to take back his teachings. He refused unless he was proved wrong by the Bible or by clear reasons.
65547.m: Luther refused to retract in Worms.

65548.q: Which sentence is attributed to Luther at Worms?
a: Here I stand, I can do no other
I came, I saw, I conquered
65548.e: The sentence has been handed down like this, even though it is not certain whether Luther said exactly these words. It stands for Luther's steadfastness.
65548.m: “Here I stand, I can do no other” is Luther's famous saying from Worms.

65549.q: Which punishment did the Edict of Worms impose on Luther in 1521?
65549.e: With the imperial ban, Luther was an outlaw: anyone could take him prisoner. His writings were also banned.
65549.m: After Worms, Luther was banned and declared an outlaw.

65550.q: In which castle was Luther hidden after the Diet of Worms?
65550.e: His ruler had Luther kidnapped in a staged attack and taken to Wartburg Castle near Eisenach. There he was safe.

65551.q: Under which false name did Luther live at Wartburg Castle?
65551.e: Luther let his hair and beard grow and lived at the castle as Junker Jörg. That way nobody recognised him.
65551.m: At Wartburg Castle, Luther was called Junker Jörg.

65552.q: What did Luther translate into German at Wartburg Castle in just a few weeks?
65552.e: In about eleven weeks, Luther translated the New Testament from Greek. It appeared in September 1522 as the September Testament.
65552.m: At Wartburg Castle, Luther translated the New Testament.

65553.q: Which ruling prince protected Luther after the Diet of Worms?
65553.e: Frederick the Wise was Elector of Saxony and Luther's ruler. He kept a protective hand over him.

65554.q: In which village in the Toggenburg was Zwingli born in 1484?
65554.e: Huldrych Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 in Wildhaus in the Toggenburg. His birthplace can be visited today.
65554.m: Zwingli came from Wildhaus in the Toggenburg.

65555.q: At which Zurich church did Zwingli work as people's priest from 1519?
65555.e: On 1 January 1519, his 35th birthday, Zwingli began preaching at the Grossmünster. He explained whole books of the Bible chapter by chapter.
65555.m: Zwingli preached in the Grossmünster in Zurich.

65556.q: Where was Zwingli people's priest immediately before he came to Zurich?
65556.e: Zwingli was first a priest in Glarus and then people's priest in the pilgrimage town of Einsiedeln. In 1519 he moved to Zurich.
65556.m: Before Zurich, Zwingli worked in Glarus and Einsiedeln.

65557.q: Which event in Zurich in 1522 is seen as the starting signal of the Reformation in Switzerland?
65557.e: At the home of the printer Froschauer, men ate sausages during Lent. Zwingli defended them, because the Lenten fast is not in the Bible.
65557.m: The sausage eating of 1522 set off the Reformation in Zurich.

65558.q: Who decided in Zurich whether the Reformation would be introduced?
65558.e: In Zurich, the city council decided after the disputations on church questions. In this way the Reformation was introduced step by step.
65558.m: In Zurich the council introduced the Reformation.

65559.q: Unlike Luther, what did the Lord's Supper mean for Zwingli?
a: A sacrificial act by the priest
65559.e: For Zwingli, the bread only signified the body of Christ. Luther believed that Christ is really present in the bread. In 1529 in Marburg they did not reach agreement.
65559.m: Zwingli saw the Lord's Supper as a sign of remembrance.

65560.q: Who became leader of the Zurich church after Zwingli's death in 1531?
65560.e: Heinrich Bullinger took over Zwingli's position at the Grossmünster in 1531. He led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

65561.q: When was the Mass abolished in Zurich and replaced by the Lord's Supper?
65561.e: At Easter 1525, Zurich celebrated the Lord's Supper in the Reformed way for the first time. The Catholic Mass was abolished.

65562.q: In which year did the famous sausage eating take place in Zurich?
65562.e: The sausage eating took place on 9 March 1522. It is seen as the beginning of the Reformation in Zurich.
65562.m: The Zurich sausage eating was in 1522.

65563.q: Which rule did the Zurich sausage eating of 1522 break?
65563.e: It was Lent, and meat was forbidden. Eating sausage together was a deliberate breaking of this rule.
65563.m: The sausage eating broke the rule of fasting.

65564.q: What was the job of Christoph Froschauer, in whose house the sausage eating took place?
65564.e: Froschauer was a well-known printer in Zurich. He later printed many writings of the Reformation.

65565.q: How did Zwingli behave at the sausage eating in 1522?
a: He was there but did not eat
He was the first to eat
He was not in Zurich at all
65565.e: Zwingli was present, but did not eat any sausage himself. Afterwards he defended the participants in public.
65565.m: Zwingli did not join in the sausage eating.

65566.q: What did Zwingli say in a sermon after the sausage eating?
a: Christians may decide for themselves what they eat
Meat is forbidden all year round
65566.e: Two weeks after the sausage eating, Zwingli preached about freedom in food. He found no rule in the Bible about fasting from meat.
65566.m: Zwingli defended freedom in what people eat.

65567.q: What reason did Froschauer give the council to excuse the sausage eating?
a: Lots of hard work on a printing order
65567.e: Froschauer explained that his journeymen had to work hard on an urgent book order and therefore needed hearty food.
65567.m: Froschauer justified the sausage eating with hard work.

65568.q: What kind of sausages were eaten at the Zurich sausage eating in 1522?
65568.e: It is recorded that two smoked sausages were cut into thin slices and shared among the guests.
65568.m: At the sausage eating there were two smoked sausages.

65569.q: Which country did the reformer John Calvin come from?
65569.e: Calvin was born in 1509 in Noyon in northern France. Because of the persecution of Protestants, he had to leave France.
65569.m: Calvin was a Frenchman from Noyon.

65570.q: In which Swiss city did John Calvin work as a reformer?
65570.e: Calvin worked in Geneva from 1536 and then again from 1541 until his death in 1564.
65570.m: Calvin was the reformer of Geneva.

65571.q: In which language did Calvin preach in Geneva?
65571.e: Calvin was French and Geneva is French-speaking. He preached and wrote in French and Latin.

65572.q: Which school did Calvin found in Geneva in 1559?
65572.e: The Geneva Academy trained ministers from all over Europe. The University of Geneva later grew out of it.
65572.m: Calvin's academy became the University of Geneva.

65573.q: What did Calvin teach about the salvation of people?
a: God has decided in advance who will be saved
You can save yourself with money
65573.e: This teaching is called predestination. Calvin stressed it especially.

65574.q: What was forbidden in Geneva in Calvin's time?
65574.e: Calvin wanted a strict, God-fearing life. Dancing, gambling and swearing were forbidden and punished in Geneva.
65574.m: Strict rules applied in Calvin's Geneva.

65575.q: What was Geneva often called because of Calvin's work?
65575.e: Geneva became a centre of the Reformed faith, to which refugees from all over Europe came. That is why it was called the Protestant Rome.
65575.m: Geneva was regarded as the Protestant Rome.

65576.q: What did the Anabaptists reject that the other churches kept?
65576.e: The Anabaptists believed that only those who believe for themselves should be baptised. That is why they baptised adults.
65576.m: Anabaptists baptised only adults who believed.

65577.q: In which city did the first adult baptism of the Anabaptist movement take place in 1525?
65577.e: On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptised Georg Blaurock in Zurich. With this, the Anabaptist movement began.
65577.m: The Anabaptist movement began in Zurich in 1525.

65578.q: Which man from Zurich was one of the founders of the Anabaptist movement?
65578.e: Conrad Grebel was at first a follower of Zwingli. But he wanted a more radical Reformation and founded the Anabaptist congregation with others.
65578.m: Conrad Grebel helped found the Anabaptist movement.

65579.q: How was the Anabaptist Felix Manz executed in Zurich in 1527?
a: He was drowned in the Limmat
65579.e: Felix Manz was drowned in the River Limmat on 5 January 1527. He was the first Anabaptist executed by the Reformed.
65579.m: Felix Manz died in the Limmat in 1527.

65580.q: What, among other things, did the Anabaptists reject in their confession of 1527?
65580.e: The confession of 1527 is called the Schleitheim Articles. The Anabaptists did not want to swear oaths or do military service.
65580.m: The Anabaptists rejected oaths and military service.

65581.q: Which man are the Amish named after?
65581.e: Jakob Ammann came from the Simmental in the canton of Bern. In 1693 he split from the other Anabaptists; his followers are called the Amish.
65581.m: The Amish are named after Jakob Ammann.

65582.q: Where did many Swiss Anabaptists flee to because of persecution?
a: To the towns on Lake Geneva
65582.e: Many Anabaptists moved to remote areas such as the Jura or emigrated to Alsace, the Palatinate and later America.
65582.m: Persecuted Anabaptists fled to the Jura and abroad.

65583.q: What is the peaceful scene during the First War of Kappel in 1529 called?
65583.e: Soldiers from both sides are said to have eaten a milk soup together. There was no battle in 1529.
65583.m: The Kappel milk soup stands for peace among the Swiss Confederates.

a: Burnt at the stake in Rome
65584.e: Zwingli went with the people of Zurich into the Second War of Kappel as an army chaplain. He was killed on 11 October 1531 at Kappel am Albis.
65584.m: Zwingli died in 1531 in the Battle of Kappel.

65585.q: Which five cantons fought on the Catholic side in the Wars of Kappel?
a: Thurgau, Aargau, St Gallen, Appenzell, the Grisons
65585.e: The five cantons of Central Switzerland stayed Catholic. They stood against Protestant Zurich.
65585.m: Central Switzerland fought at Kappel for the old faith.

65586.q: How did Zurich put pressure on the Catholic cantons before the Second War of Kappel?
a: With a ban on cheese imports
65586.e: In 1531 Zurich and Bern stopped deliveries of grain and salt to Central Switzerland. The Catholic cantons then attacked.
65586.m: A food blockade led to the Second War of Kappel.

65587.q: What did the Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 decide?
a: Each canton chooses its own faith
65587.e: Each canton was allowed to decide its own religion. So Switzerland stayed divided by religion.
65587.m: After Kappel, each canton chose its own faith.

65588.q: Which canton is Kappel am Albis in?
65588.e: Kappel am Albis is in the canton of Zurich near the border with the canton of Zug. A monument recalls Zwingli's death.
65588.m: Kappel am Albis is in the canton of Zurich.

65589.q: What does iconoclasm mean in the Reformation?
65589.e: Many Protestants thought that pictures and statues in churches led people to worship idols. So they were removed or destroyed.
65589.m: During iconoclasm, images disappeared from churches.

65590.q: Which commandment did the Protestants refer to when they removed the images?
a: You shall not make for yourself an image
65590.e: The ban on images in the Ten Commandments was very important to Zwingli and Calvin. That is why Protestant churches are often plain.
65590.m: Protestant churches are plain because of the ban on images.

65591.q: How were the images removed from the churches in Zurich in 1524?
a: In an orderly way by decision of the council
By a wild crowd at night
65591.e: The Zurich council had the images removed in an orderly way in the summer of 1524. So it was more of a planned clearance than a wild riot.
65591.m: In Zurich the council cleared the images from the churches in an orderly way.

65592.q: In which Swiss city was there a violent outbreak of iconoclasm in 1529, after which the Reformation was introduced?
65592.e: In February 1529 supporters of the Reformation in Basel destroyed many images in the minster and other churches. After that the Reformation was introduced.
65592.m: Basel saw a great outbreak of iconoclasm in 1529.

65593.q: What do Protestant churches in Switzerland usually look like inside?
a: Plain and without pictures of saints
65593.e: After the Reformation, pictures and altars were removed. The pulpit and the Word of God are at the centre.

65594.q: Where was Martin Luther hiding when images were removed from churches in Wittenberg in 1522?
65594.e: Luther lived in hiding at Wartburg Castle and translated the New Testament there. Others such as Karlstadt pushed ahead with removing images in Wittenberg.
65594.m: In 1522 Luther was hiding at Wartburg Castle.

65595.q: What was often also removed from Protestant churches during iconoclasm?
65595.e: Zwingli rejected music in church services, so the organs were also removed in Zurich. They only came back much later.
65595.m: In Zurich the organs also disappeared with the Reformation.

a: A short printed booklet on one topic
A letter brought by a pigeon
65596.e: Pamphlets were cheap booklets with only a few pages. During the Reformation they spread new ideas quickly across the country.

65597.q: Why did printing help the Reformation so much?
a: It caused books to be banned
Printed copies cost more than handwritten ones
65597.e: With printing, Luther's writings could be produced in large numbers. So they reached many people in a short time.
65597.m: Without printing, the Reformation would have spread more slowly.

65598.q: Which complete German Bible was published first?
65598.e: The Zurich Bible was published in 1531 by Christoph Froschauer. Luther's complete Bible only followed in 1534.
65598.m: The Zurich Bible came out in 1531, before the Luther Bible.

65599.q: Why was Luther's translation of the Bible so important?
a: Many people could now read the Bible in German
It was the very first Bible
It was meant only for priests
65599.e: Luther's complete Bible came out in 1534. His clear language had a strong influence on the German language.
65599.m: Luther translated the Bible into clear German.

65600.q: How did Martin Luther's face become known everywhere in his time?
65600.e: The painter Lucas Cranach, a friend of Luther's, made many portraits and woodcuts. Once printed, they spread quickly.

65601.q: In which language did Luther write many of his works so that ordinary people could read them too?
65601.e: Scholars at that time usually wrote in Latin. Luther wrote many works in German, for example ‘On the Freedom of a Christian’ in 1520.
65601.m: Luther wrote in German for ordinary people.

65602.q: How widespread were Luther's writings compared with other authors of his time?
a: He was the most printed author
He was only printed in Latin
65602.e: Luther was the most printed author of his time in the German-speaking world. His writings appeared in very large numbers of copies.
65602.m: Luther was the most printed author of his time.

65603.q: What was the Council of Trent the Catholic Church's answer to?
65603.e: The council met from 1545 to 1563. It was meant to clarify Catholic teaching and put right abuses.
65603.m: The Council of Trent responded to the Reformation.

65604.q: How many sacraments did the Council of Trent confirm?
65604.e: The council kept seven sacraments, such as baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist and marriage. The Protestants only recognised baptism and Holy Communion.
65604.m: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments.

65605.q: What is the renewal of the Catholic Church after the Council of Trent called?
65605.e: People speak of the Counter-Reformation or the Catholic Reform. The Church wanted to put right abuses and win back lost areas.

65606.q: Which institution for training priests did the Council of Trent call for?
65606.e: The council required every diocese to have a seminary. That way priests would be better trained.

65607.q: Which translation of the Bible did the Council of Trent declare authoritative?
65607.e: The Vulgate is the Latin translation of the Bible that goes back to Jerome. It was the official text in the Catholic Church.
65607.m: For Trent the Latin Vulgate was authoritative.

65608.q: Which Archbishop of Milan also put the decisions of Trent into practice in Switzerland?
65608.e: Charles Borromeo visited the Catholic areas of Switzerland and promoted reforms. At his suggestion a papal nuncio came to Lucerne.
65608.m: Charles Borromeo brought the reforms of Trent to Switzerland.

65610.q: What do the letters SJ after a Jesuit's name stand for?
65610.e: Societas Jesu is Latin and means Society of Jesus. That is the official name of the order.

65611.q: In which Swiss town did the Jesuits found the College of St Michael?
65611.e: The Jesuit Peter Canisius founded the College of St Michael in Fribourg. The school still exists today.
65611.m: The College of St Michael is in Fribourg.

65612.q: What did the Swiss Federal Constitution say about the Jesuits until 1973?
a: They had to do military service
They were allowed to elect the Federal Council
65612.e: The ban on Jesuits had been in the Federal Constitution since 1848. It was lifted in a popular vote in 1973.
65612.m: Until 1973 the Jesuits were banned in Switzerland.

65613.q: What were the Jesuits especially known for during the Counter-Reformation?
65613.e: The Jesuits founded many grammar schools and colleges. In this way they trained Catholic leaders.

65614.q: Which pope was the first Jesuit on the Chair of Saint Peter?
65614.e: Pope Francis, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, was elected in 2013. He was the first pope from the Jesuit order.
65614.m: Francis was the first Jesuit pope.

65615.q: In which city is the great Reformation Wall with Calvin and Farel?
65615.e: The monument stands against the old city wall of Geneva. It recalls the reformers who shaped Geneva.
65615.m: The Reformation Wall is in Geneva.

65616.q: What was the Reformation Wall in Geneva built against?
65616.e: The monument stands against the old city wall in the Parc des Bastions. The University of Geneva is next to it.
65616.m: The Reformation Wall stands against Geneva's old city wall.

65617.q: Which Latin motto is written above the Reformation Wall in Geneva?
65617.e: Post Tenebras Lux means ‘After darkness, light’. It is Geneva's motto and also appears on Geneva's coat of arms.
65617.m: Post Tenebras Lux is Geneva's motto.

65618.q: Which reformer stands in the middle of the Reformation Wall in Geneva?
65618.e: The four large figures show Farel, Calvin, Beza and Knox. Calvin shaped the Reformation in Geneva most strongly.
65618.m: Calvin stands in the middle of the Reformation Wall in Geneva.

65619.q: About how long is the Reformation Wall in Geneva?
65619.e: The wall of the monument is about 100 metres long. It was built from stone from Burgundy.
65619.m: The Reformation Wall in Geneva is about 100 metres long.

65620.q: For what occasion was the foundation stone of the Reformation Wall in Geneva laid in 1909?
a: The founding of the Swiss Confederation
65620.e: Calvin was born in 1509. The foundation stone was laid in July 1909 for his 400th birthday, and the monument was opened in 1917.
65620.m: The foundation stone was laid for Calvin's 400th birthday.

65621.q: How are Luther and Zwingli honoured on the Reformation Wall in Geneva?
a: With their names carved in stone
With large statues in the middle
65621.e: The names Luther and Zwingli are carved into stones beside the steps. The large statues, on the other hand, show Geneva's reformers.
65621.m: Luther and Zwingli appear as names on the Geneva monument.

65622.q: What was added to the Reformation Wall in Geneva in 2002?
65622.e: In 2002 the name of Marie Dentière was carved into it. She worked for the Reformation in Geneva and is the first woman on the monument.
65622.m: Since 2002 a woman has also been named on the Reformation Wall in Geneva.

65623.q: Where is the Roman Curia, which helps the pope lead the Church, based?
65623.e: The Curia is made up of different offices in the Vatican. It helps the pope lead and run the worldwide Church.
65623.m: The Roman Curia works in the Vatican.

65624.q: What is the meeting of cardinals that elects a new pope called?
65624.e: The word conclave comes from the Latin ‘cum clave’, meaning ‘with a key’, because the cardinals are locked in while they vote. White smoke shows that a new pope has been elected.
65624.m: In the conclave the cardinals elect the pope.

65625.q: What colour do cardinals wear on special occasions?
65625.e: The cardinals' red recalls the blood of the martyrs. It shows that they should be ready to give their lives for the faith.

65627.q: How many dioceses does the Roman Catholic Church have in Switzerland?
65627.e: The six dioceses are Basel, Chur, Lausanne-Geneva-Fribourg, Lugano, St Gallen and Sion. There are also the territorial abbeys of Einsiedeln and Saint-Maurice.
65627.m: Catholic Switzerland is divided into six dioceses.

65628.q: Who was elected pope in May 2025?
65628.e: On 8 May 2025 the American Robert Francis Prevost was elected and took the name Leo XIV. He is the first pope from the USA (as of 2025).
65628.m: Leo XIV has been pope since 2025.

65629.q: What changed in the Catholic Mass after the Second Vatican Council (1962 to 1965)?
a: It could be celebrated in the local language
It was only celebrated in Latin
Only bishops were allowed to celebrate it
65629.e: Before, Mass was almost only celebrated in Latin. After the council it could be celebrated in people's own language, for example in German.
65629.m: Since the Second Vatican Council, Mass has been held in the local language.

65630.q: What is the rule that Catholic priests must not marry called?
65630.e: In the Roman Catholic Church, priests of the Latin rite are usually not allowed to marry. This way of life is called celibacy.

65631.q: After which religious debate did Bern introduce the Reformation in 1528?
65631.e: At the Bern Disputation in January 1528, theologians debated questions of faith. After that Bern decided to introduce the Reformation.
65631.m: With the Bern Disputation, Bern became Protestant in 1528.

65632.q: Which two sacraments does the Reformed Church recognise?
65632.e: The Reformed Church only recognises sacraments that, according to the Bible, Jesus himself set up. These are baptism and Holy Communion.
65632.m: The Reformed Church celebrates baptism and Holy Communion as sacraments.

65634.q: Where did Huldrych Zwingli die in 1531?
65634.e: In the Second War of Kappel, Protestants from Zurich fought against Catholic cantons. Zwingli was killed as an army chaplain at Kappel am Albis in 1531.
65634.m: Zwingli died in 1531 in the Battle of Kappel.

65635.q: Why are Protestant churches usually plain and without pictures of saints?
a: Images were removed during the Reformation
Pictures were too expensive at the time
The churches are all very new
65635.e: During the Reformation, pictures and statues were removed from churches in Zurich and other places. The Word of God was to be at the centre.
65635.m: Protestant churches put the Word, not images, at the centre.

65636.q: What has the national union of the Reformed churches of Switzerland been called since 2020?
65636.e: Since 2020 the union of the Reformed cantonal churches has been called the Protestant Church in Switzerland (EKS). Before that it was called the Federation of Swiss Protestant Churches.
65636.m: The EKS unites the Reformed churches of Switzerland.

65637.q: What is the monument to the reformers in the Parc des Bastions in Geneva called?
65637.e: The Reformation Wall in Geneva is a long wall with large figures of Calvin, Farel, Beza and Knox. It was begun in 1909 for Calvin's 400th birthday.
65637.m: The Reformation Wall in Geneva honours the reformers.

65639.q: Which patriarch has a primacy of honour in the Orthodox Church?
65639.e: The Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople (today Istanbul) is regarded as ‘first among equals’. But he is not a head like the pope.
65639.m: The Patriarch of Constantinople is first among equals.

65640.q: Which Orthodox church has the most members?
65640.e: The Russian Orthodox Church has by far the most believers. It is led by the Patriarch of Moscow.
65640.m: The Russian church is the largest Orthodox church.

65641.q: What does the Greek word ‘orthodoxy’ mean?
65641.e: Orthodoxy is made up of ‘orthos’ meaning right and ‘doxa’ meaning opinion or praise. The Church sees itself as the guardian of the true faith.

65642.q: Why do many Orthodox Christians celebrate Christmas on 7 January?
a: The Three Wise Men came then
December is a time of fasting
65642.e: Many Orthodox churches date church festivals by the old Julian calendar. Today it is 13 days behind our Gregorian calendar.
65642.m: The Julian calendar moves Orthodox Christmas into January.

65643.q: Which peninsula in Greece is a famous monastic state of the Orthodox Church?
65643.e: On Mount Athos, Orthodox monks have lived in about 20 monasteries for more than 1000 years. Women are not allowed to set foot on the peninsula.
65643.m: Mount Athos is the heart of Orthodox monastic life.

65644.q: What is the main Sunday service in the Orthodox Church called?
65644.e: The Divine Liturgy is the Orthodox celebration of the Eucharist. The best-known form goes back to John Chrysostom.
65644.m: Orthodox Christians celebrate the Divine Liturgy on Sundays.

65645.q: Under what condition may Orthodox priests be married?
65645.e: In the Orthodox Church a man may marry before he is ordained a priest. Bishops, however, are only chosen from unmarried monks.
65645.m: Orthodox priests may marry if they do so before ordination.

65646.q: What does the Greek word ‘eikon’, from which ‘icon’ comes, mean?
65646.e: An icon is a holy picture, usually of Christ, Mary or saints. The Greek word ‘eikon’ means image or likeness.

65647.q: What material are icons traditionally painted on?
65647.e: Classic icons are painted on prepared wooden panels. The panel is first coated with a chalk ground.

65648.q: What is the wall covered with icons in front of the sanctuary of Orthodox churches called?
65648.e: The iconostasis separates the sanctuary from the area for the faithful. It has three doors that the priest goes through during the liturgy.
65648.m: The iconostasis is a wall of pictures in front of the altar.

65649.q: What does the golden background of many icons represent?
65649.e: In icons, gold stands for the light of God and the heavenly world. This means the figures do not seem to be in an earthly landscape.
65649.m: On icons, gold shows heavenly light.

65650.q: What was the dispute in the Byzantine Empire over whether holy images could be venerated called?
65650.e: In the 8th and 9th centuries icons were at times banned and destroyed. In 843 the veneration of images was finally allowed, which the Orthodox Church still celebrates today.
65650.m: The Iconoclastic Controversy ended with icons being allowed.

65651.e: Icons are holy pictures. They usually show Christ, Mary the Mother of God or saints.
65651.m: Icons show Jesus, Mary and saints.

65652.q: Which kitchen ingredient do icon painters traditionally mix their paints with?
65652.e: The colour pigments are bound with egg yolk. This way of painting is called egg tempera and lasts a very long time.
65652.m: Icon painters bind their paints with egg yolk.

65653.q: Which English king separated the Church of England from Rome in 1534?
65653.e: Henry VIII wanted his marriage annulled, which the pope refused. With the Act of Supremacy of 1534 he made himself head of the Church of England.
65653.m: Henry VIII separated the English Church from Rome.

65654.q: Who is the most important clergyman of the Church of England?
65654.e: The Archbishop of Canterbury is the highest-ranking bishop of the Church of England. He is also seen as the spiritual focus of the worldwide Anglican Communion.
65654.m: Canterbury is the most important bishop's seat for Anglicans.

65655.q: Who is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England?
65655.e: Since the Reformation under Henry VIII, the king or queen has formally been at the head of the Church of England. Today that is King Charles III (as of 2026).
65655.m: The British king is head of the established Church of England.

65656.q: In which language did the Church of England hold its services after the break with Rome?
65656.e: With the Book of Common Prayer of 1549, services were held in English. Before that they were in Latin.
65656.m: Anglicans hold their services in English.

65657.q: In which Anglican church in London are British kings and queens crowned?
65657.e: Coronations have taken place in Westminster Abbey since 1066. King Charles III was also crowned there in 2023.
65657.m: British monarchs are crowned in Westminster Abbey.

65658.q: Where does the Anglican Church get its name from?
65658.e: ‘Anglican’ comes from the Latin ‘anglicanus’, English. The Church began in England.

65659.q: Why are there also Anglican churches in Kenya, Australia or Canada?
65659.e: The Anglican Church came to the colonies with the British. Today these churches together form the worldwide Anglican Communion.
65659.m: Anglican churches are found mainly in former British colonies.

65660.q: Which church did the Christian Catholics break away from in the 19th century?
65660.e: In 1870 the First Vatican Council declared the pope infallible in matters of faith. Catholics who rejected this founded their own churches.
65660.m: The Christian Catholics broke away from Rome.

65661.q: In which city is the seat of the bishop of the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland?
65661.e: The Christian Catholic bishop has his seat in Bern. The Church was organised in 1875 as the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland.
65661.m: The Christian Catholic bishop works in Bern.

65662.q: What are the Christian Catholics usually called outside Switzerland?
65662.e: In Germany, Austria and the Netherlands people speak of Old Catholic churches. In Switzerland the same branch of faith is called Christian Catholic.
65662.m: Christian Catholic and Old Catholic mean the same branch.

65663.q: Who leads the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland?
65663.e: The Christian Catholics do not accept the pope as their head. They have their own bishop and internationally belong to the Union of Utrecht.
65663.m: The Christian Catholics have their own bishop.

65664.q: Since when has the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland existed?
65664.e: The Church was organised in 1875. In 1876 Eduard Herzog became its first bishop.
65664.m: The Christian Catholic Church began in the 19th century.

65665.q: What makes Christian Catholic priests different from Roman Catholic ones?
a: They do not celebrate the Eucharist
65665.e: In the Christian Catholic Church there is no rule of celibacy. Women can also be ordained as priests.
65665.m: Christian Catholic priests may be married.

65666.q: What status does the Christian Catholic Church have in many cantons?
a: It is recognised as an official church
It is the federal state church
It has no rights as a church
65666.e: Alongside the Roman Catholic and the Reformed Church, the Christian Catholic Church is officially recognised under public law in several cantons. But it is the smallest of these three official churches.
65666.m: The Christian Catholic Church is an official church in several cantons.

65667.q: What happened to the language of services among the Christian Catholics as early as the 19th century?
a: Latin was replaced by the local language
65667.e: The Christian Catholics held services in the local language instead of Latin early on. The Roman Catholic Church only did this after 1965.
65667.m: Christian Catholics worshipped in their mother tongue early on.

65668.q: Which Latin principle of Luther's says that the Bible alone is the standard of faith?
65668.e: ‘Sola scriptura’ means ‘Scripture alone’. For Luther the Bible stood above the traditions and decisions of the Church.
65668.m: Sola scriptura means that Scripture alone counts.

65669.q: What were Luther's 95 Theses mainly directed against?
65669.e: With letters of indulgence, people could supposedly buy their way out of punishment for sins. Luther criticised the fact that forgiveness had become a business.
65669.m: Luther criticised the sale of indulgences.

65670.q: Which well-known hymn did Martin Luther write?
65670.e: Luther wrote many hymns so that the congregation could sing in German during services. ‘A Mighty Fortress Is Our God’ was written around 1529 and became the hymn of the Reformation.
65670.m: Luther wanted the whole congregation to sing.

65671.q: What is the most important Lutheran confession of 1530 called?
65671.e: The Augsburg Confession (Confessio Augustana) was presented to the emperor at the Imperial Diet in Augsburg in 1530. It sums up the Lutheran faith.
65671.m: The Augsburg Confession is the foundation of the Lutherans.

65672.q: In which Swiss city is the Lutheran World Federation based?
65672.e: The Lutheran World Federation was founded in 1947 and is based at the Ecumenical Centre in Geneva. It unites Lutheran churches from many countries.
65672.m: The Lutheran World Federation is based in Geneva.

65673.q: In which region of Europe are most people Lutheran?
65673.e: In Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland the Lutheran Church is the largest church. In some countries it was the state church for a long time.

65674.q: What is Martin Luther's emblem with a cross, a heart and a rose called?
65674.e: In 1530 Luther had a seal made with a black cross in a red heart on a white rose. Today it is a symbol of many Lutheran churches.
65674.m: The Luther rose is the symbol of the Lutherans.

65675.q: At which Imperial Diet did Luther refuse to take back his writings in 1521?
65675.e: In front of Emperor Charles V, Luther refused to recant in Worms in 1521. After that he was declared an outlaw of the Empire.
65675.m: At Worms, Luther stood by his teaching.

65676.q: What is a typical feature of a free church?
a: It is independent of the state
It is paid for by the canton
You are automatically a member from birth
65676.e: Free churches receive no church taxes and are funded by voluntary donations. You become a member consciously and by choice.
65676.m: Free churches are independent of the state.

65677.q: Which free church holds its weekly service on Saturday?
65677.e: As in the Bible, the Seventh-day Adventists keep the seventh day, the Sabbath, as a day of rest. That is why they hold their service on Saturday instead of Sunday.
65677.m: Adventists keep the Sabbath on Saturday.

65678.q: What are the leaders of a Salvation Army congregation called?
65678.e: The Salvation Army is organised like an army, and its members wear uniforms. That is why the leaders of a congregation have military titles and are called officers.
65678.m: In the Salvation Army, officers lead the congregations.

65679.q: Who did William Booth mainly want to help with the Salvation Army?
65679.e: William Booth founded the movement in 1865 in the poor East End of London. He looked after hungry and homeless people and people without work.
65679.m: The Salvation Army helps poor people.

65680.q: Which free church goes back to the Anabaptist movement that began in Zurich around 1525?
65680.e: The Anabaptist movement began around 1525 in the setting of the Zurich Reformation and was persecuted for a long time. The Mennonites got their name from the Frisian theologian Menno Simons.
65680.m: The Mennonites descend from the Zurich Anabaptists.

65681.q: Who do many free churches baptise?
a: People who decide for the faith themselves
65681.e: Many free churches only baptise people who declare for themselves that they believe in Jesus. This believers' baptism goes back to the Anabaptists.
65681.m: Many free churches only baptise people who decide for themselves.

65682.q: In which city was the free church ICF founded in 1996?
65682.e: ICF stands for International Christian Fellowship and began in Zurich in 1996. Today there are ICF churches in many countries.
65682.m: The free church ICF comes from Zurich.

a: Only people who believe for themselves
All the people of a village
65683.e: Baptists reject infant baptism and only baptise people who declare their faith themselves. This is called believers' baptism.

65684.e: In Baptist baptism, the whole body is briefly dipped under water. The Greek word ‘baptizein’ means to dip.

65685.q: Where do Baptists get their name from?
a: From the Greek word for baptise
From the Latin word for pray
65685.e: The Greek word ‘baptizein’ means to dip or to baptise. Baptism is especially important to Baptists.

65686.q: Which famous civil rights leader was pastor of a Baptist church?
65686.e: Martin Luther King was pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery. He fought without violence for the rights of Black people in the USA.
65686.m: Martin Luther King was a Baptist pastor.

65687.q: Which country has the most Baptists?
65687.e: The Southern Baptist Convention in the USA is the largest Protestant church in the country. Baptists are especially widespread in the southern USA.
65687.m: Most Baptists live in the USA.

65688.q: Who decides on the affairs of a congregation among Baptists?
65688.e: Baptist congregations are independent and settle their affairs at the church meeting. This principle is called congregationalism.
65688.m: Each Baptist congregation decides for itself.

65689.q: Which large group of churches do the Baptists belong to?
65689.e: The Baptists are a Protestant free church. They came out of the Reformation in the 17th century.
65689.m: Baptists belong to the Protestant churches.

65690.q: What did the Baptist preacher Billy Graham become known for around the world?
a: A new translation of the Bible
65690.e: In the 20th century Billy Graham held large faith events in many countries. Altogether he preached to over 200 million people.
65690.m: Billy Graham preached to millions of people.

65691.q: Who is regarded as the founder of Methodism?
65691.e: John Wesley was an Anglican priest in 18th-century England. His revival movement became Methodism.

65692.q: Where does Methodism get its name from?
a: From an orderly, methodical way of life
65692.e: Students around the Wesley brothers in Oxford lived by strict rules with prayer, Bible reading and help for the poor. So people who mocked them called them Methodists.
65692.m: Methodists got their name from their orderly way of life.

65693.q: What did Charles Wesley, the brother of the founder of Methodism, write in large numbers?
65693.e: Charles Wesley wrote over 6000 hymns. Many of them are still sung in English-speaking churches today.
65693.m: Charles Wesley was the hymn writer of the Methodists.

65694.q: What is the Methodist church in Switzerland called?
65694.e: In Switzerland the Methodists are organised in the Evangelical Methodist Church (EMK). It belongs to the worldwide United Methodist Church.
65694.m: In Switzerland the Methodists are called the EMK.

65695.q: Where did John Wesley often preach because many churches would not let him?
65695.e: Wesley gave many open-air sermons to workers and miners. In this way he reached people who rarely went to church.

65696.q: Which church did Methodism come from?
65696.e: John Wesley remained a priest of the Church of England all his life. Only after his death did the Methodists separate from it completely.
65696.m: Methodism began within the Anglican Church.

65697.q: What did the Methodists campaign for especially early on?
a: For the poor and against slavery
65697.e: Wesley cared for prisoners, the sick and the poor and strongly criticised slavery. Social action is still part of Methodism today.
65697.m: Methodists combine faith with helping the disadvantaged.

65698.q: What does the name of the Pentecostal movement recall?
a: The miracle of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came
65698.e: Pentecostal churches stress the gifts of the Holy Spirit. They refer to the miracle of Pentecost described in the Acts of the Apostles.
65698.m: The Pentecostal movement is named after the miracle of Pentecost.

65699.q: Apart from speaking in tongues, which spiritual gift is especially important in Pentecostal churches?
65699.e: Pentecostal churches often pray for the sick and expect healing through God's power. They refer to accounts in the New Testament.
65699.m: Pentecostals often pray for the sick to be healed.

65700.q: In which country did the Pentecostal movement get a big boost at the beginning of the 20th century?
65700.e: From 1906 many people came to services on Azusa Street in Los Angeles. From there the Pentecostal movement spread around the world.
65700.m: The Pentecostal movement got a big boost in the USA.

65701.q: What was very unusual at the time about the first Pentecostal services in Los Angeles?
a: Black and white people prayed together
Only children were allowed to come
65701.e: The African American preacher William J. Seymour led the services. In the USA around 1906 it was very rare for Black and white people to pray together.
65701.m: In Los Angeles, Black and white people prayed together.

65702.q: What is praying in unknown languages, as found in Pentecostal churches, called?
65702.e: Speaking in tongues, also called glossolalia, is seen in Pentecostal churches as a gift of the Holy Spirit. It is already mentioned in the Bible.
65702.m: Speaking in tongues is praying in an unknown language.

65703.q: Where is the Pentecostal movement growing especially fast today?
65703.e: The Pentecostal movement is one of the fastest-growing Christian movements in the world. It has especially many followers in Brazil, Nigeria and other countries of the global South.
65703.m: The Pentecostal movement is growing mainly in Latin America and Africa.

65704.q: Roughly how many people around the world belong to the Pentecostal movement and similar movements today?
65704.e: The Pentecostal movement is one of the fastest-growing Christian movements. Together with related groups it has several hundred million followers.
65704.m: The Pentecostal movement has hundreds of millions of followers worldwide.

65705.q: What is a large association of Pentecostal churches in Switzerland called?
65705.e: The Swiss Pentecostal Mission (SPM) unites many Pentecostal churches in Switzerland. It is one of the larger free church associations in the country.
65705.m: The Swiss Pentecostal Mission unites many Pentecostal churches.

65706.q: In which country do the great majority of Coptic Christians live?
65706.e: The Copts are the largest Christian community in Egypt. The word ‘Copt’ comes from the Greek word for Egyptian.
65706.m: The Copts are the Christians of Egypt.

65707.q: According to tradition, which evangelist founded the Church in Alexandria?
65707.e: According to Coptic tradition, the evangelist Mark brought the Christian faith to Alexandria. That is why the Church is also called the ‘Church of Saint Mark’.
65707.m: The Copts trace their Church back to Mark.

65708.q: What title does the head of the Coptic Orthodox Church have?
65708.e: The head of the Copts is called Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of Saint Mark. Since 2012 this has been Tawadros II (as of 2026).
65708.m: The Copts also call their head pope.

65709.q: According to its tradition, roughly how old is the Coptic Church?
65709.e: The Copts trace their Church back to the evangelist Mark in the 1st century. It is one of the oldest churches in the world.
65709.m: The Coptic Church is almost 2000 years old.

65710.q: Which language is still used in the Coptic liturgy today?
65710.e: Coptic is the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language and is written with an alphabet based mainly on Greek letters. It is no longer spoken in everyday life, but it is used in church services.
65710.m: Coptic lives on in the liturgy.

65711.q: Which Egyptian saint is regarded as the father of Christian monasticism?
65711.e: Anthony lived as a hermit in the Egyptian desert in the 3rd and 4th centuries. Many followed his example, and that is how monasticism began.
65711.m: Christian monasticism began in the Egyptian desert.

65712.q: What do many Copts wear on their wrist as a visible sign of their faith?
65712.e: Many Copts have a small cross tattooed on the inside of their wrist when they are still children. It shows that they belong to the Church.
65712.m: The cross on the wrist is a sign of many Copts.

65713.q: What does the Greek word ‘oikoumene’ mean?
65713.e: In ancient times ‘oikoumene’ meant the whole inhabited world. Today ecumenism means the effort for cooperation and unity among the Christian churches.
65713.m: Ecumenism originally means the whole inhabited world.

65714.q: In which city is the World Council of Churches based?
65714.e: The World Council of Churches (WCC) is based in Geneva. It unites more than 300 churches from all over the world.
65714.m: The World Council of Churches is based in Geneva.

65715.q: In which year was the World Council of Churches founded?
65715.e: The World Council of Churches was founded in 1948 at an assembly in Amsterdam. That was shortly after the Second World War.
65715.m: The World Council of Churches has existed since 1948.

65716.q: Which large church is not a full member of the World Council of Churches?
65716.e: The Roman Catholic Church works closely with the WCC but is not a member. It sends observers and members to some commissions.
65716.m: The Catholic Church works with the World Council of Churches without being a member.

65717.q: When does the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity take place each year?
a: In the first week of Advent
65717.e: In the northern hemisphere the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity is held from 18 to 25 January. Churches of different denominations pray together.
65717.m: In January, Christians pray for their unity for a week.

65718.q: Which ecumenical community in France did the Swiss Brother Roger found?
65718.e: Brother Roger Schutz founded the Taizé Community in Burgundy in 1940. Every year thousands of young people from many denominations go there.
65718.m: Taizé is a meeting place for young people of all denominations.

65719.q: Which two churches reached agreement in Augsburg in 1999 on an old dispute from the time of the Reformation?
65719.e: In 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church signed a joint declaration. This largely settled an important dispute from Luther's time.
65719.m: Catholics and Lutherans found a shared view in 1999.

65720.q: Which two churches withdrew their mutual condemnations from the Middle Ages in 1965?
a: The Catholic and the Orthodox Church
The Reformed and the Lutheran Church
The Anglican and the Methodist Church
The Coptic and the Armenian Church
65720.e: In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the excommunications from the year 1054. That was an important step towards reconciling the Western and Eastern Churches.
65720.m: Since 1965 the old excommunications between Rome and Constantinople have been lifted.

65721.q: What is the ecumenical association of Christian churches in Switzerland called?
a: Council of Christian Churches in Switzerland
65721.e: In the Council of Christian Churches in Switzerland (AGCK), Catholic, Reformed, Christian Catholic, Orthodox and other churches work together. It was founded in 1971.
65721.m: The AGCK connects the churches of Switzerland.

65722.q: Which sacrament may also be validly given by a person who is not ordained in an emergency?
65722.e: When a life is in danger, anyone may carry out an emergency baptism by pouring water over the head and saying the words of baptism.
65722.m: In an emergency, anyone may baptise.

65723.q: How many sacraments does the Catholic Church have?
65723.e: The seven sacraments are baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, ordination and marriage.
65723.m: The Catholic Church has seven sacraments.

65724.q: With which sacrament is a person received into the Church?
65724.e: Baptism is the first sacrament. Through it a person becomes a member of the Church. Confirmation and the Eucharist follow later.
65724.m: You are received into the Church through baptism.

65725.q: How is a sacrament often briefly described?
a: A visible sign of God's invisible grace
A hymn in a church service
65725.e: Augustine already described sacraments as visible signs of an invisible reality, for example water in baptism.
65725.m: A sacrament lets people experience God's closeness through a visible sign.

65726.q: Which sacrament has three levels: deacon, priest and bishop?
65726.e: The sacrament of holy orders is given in three levels: ordination as a deacon, as a priest and as a bishop.
65726.m: Ordination has the levels deacon, priest and bishop.

65727.q: According to Catholic teaching, who gives the sacrament of marriage?
a: The bride and groom to each other
65727.e: In the Latin Church, the bride and groom give the sacrament to each other. The priest or deacon is present as the Church's witness.
65727.m: At a Catholic wedding, the couple give the sacrament to each other.

65728.q: Which three Catholic sacraments can you only receive once in your life?
a: Confirmation, marriage, anointing of the sick
65728.e: According to Catholic teaching, baptism, confirmation and ordination leave an indelible mark and are therefore not repeated.
65728.m: Baptism, confirmation and ordination are received only once.

65729.q: How many sacraments do the Reformed churches have?
65729.e: The reformers only recognised baptism and Holy Communion as sacraments. The Catholic Church, on the other hand, kept seven sacraments.
65729.m: The Reformed churches have two sacraments: baptism and Holy Communion.

65730.q: What does the Greek word ‘mysterion’, which Orthodox Christians use for the sacraments, mean?
65730.e: Mysterion means mystery or secret. That is why the Eastern Churches call the sacraments mysteries.

65731.q: What does the Greek word ‘Eucharist’ mean?
65731.e: Eucharistia means thanksgiving in Greek. At the Last Supper Jesus said the prayer of thanks over the bread and wine.

65732.q: What is the thin, round bread given at Catholic communion called?
65732.e: The host is made of unleavened wheat dough. The name comes from the Latin ‘hostia’, meaning offering.
65732.m: At communion, Catholics receive the host.

65733.q: What is the decorated cabinet in Catholic churches where the consecrated hosts are kept called?
65733.e: The consecrated hosts are kept in the tabernacle, for example for communion for the sick. The word comes from the Latin ‘tabernaculum’, meaning tent.
65733.m: The consecrated hosts are kept in the tabernacle.

65734.q: What does the ‘sanctuary lamp’ in a Catholic church show?
a: There are consecrated hosts in the tabernacle
The service is about to begin
65734.e: The sanctuary lamp, usually red, burns all the time near the tabernacle and shows the presence of Christ in the Eucharistic bread.
65734.m: The sanctuary lamp shows that hosts are kept in the tabernacle.

65735.q: How long should Catholics go without eating before receiving communion?
65735.e: Since 1964 Church law has required a Eucharistic fast of one hour. Water and medicine are allowed.
65735.m: Before communion you fast for one hour.

65736.q: What is the chalice used for at Mass?
65736.e: At Mass the wine is offered in the chalice. The hosts, on the other hand, lie in a bowl or in the ciborium.
65736.m: At Mass the wine is in the chalice.

65737.q: What are Jesus' words ‘This is my body’, spoken at Mass and Holy Communion, called?
65737.e: With the words of institution, the Church remembers how Jesus gave bread and wine at the Last Supper.
65737.m: The words of institution recall the Last Supper.

65738.q: How did Huldrych Zwingli understand Holy Communion?
a: As a memorial meal that remembers Jesus
As a sacrifice needed every day
As a feast only for priests
65738.e: Zwingli read the word ‘is’ as ‘means’: bread and wine are signs that recall Jesus' death.
65738.m: For Zwingli, Holy Communion was above all a meal of remembrance.

65739.q: What could Luther and Zwingli not agree on in 1529?
65739.e: At the Marburg Colloquy, Luther and Zwingli agreed on many points, but not on how to understand the bread and wine in Holy Communion.
65739.m: Luther and Zwingli argued about Holy Communion.

65740.q: In which Zurich church did Huldrych Zwingli preach?
65740.e: Zwingli was pastor at the Grossmünster in Zurich. There, in 1525, Holy Communion was celebrated in Reformed form for the first time.
65740.m: Zwingli preached in the Grossmünster in Zurich.

65741.q: What do the faithful receive at Reformed Holy Communion?
a: Bread and wine or grape juice
65741.e: Reformed congregations share bread and wine. Grape juice is often offered too, so that children and people who do not drink alcohol can take part.
65741.m: At Holy Communion the congregation shares bread and wine or grape juice.

65742.q: What did Martin Luther teach about the bread and wine in Holy Communion?
a: Christ is really present in them
They are only signs without meaning
65742.e: Luther held to the real presence of Christ ‘in, with and under’ the bread and wine, without taking over the Catholic teaching of transformation.
65742.m: Luther believed in the real presence of Christ in Holy Communion.

65743.q: What was important to the reformers at Holy Communion that was hardly usual for lay people in the Middle Ages?
65743.e: In the late Middle Ages lay people usually only received the host. The reformers gave the bread and the cup to all the faithful.
65743.m: The Reformation gave the cup back to all the faithful.

65744.q: What vessels were used to give out Holy Communion in Zurich after the Reformation, to avoid splendour?
65744.e: Zwingli wanted simplicity, so in Zurich plain wooden cups and plates were used instead of golden chalices.
65744.m: Zurich deliberately celebrated Holy Communion with simple wooden vessels.

65745.q: What else is the sacrament of confession called in the Catholic Church today?
65745.e: Confession is also called the sacrament of penance or the sacrament of reconciliation, because it brings reconciliation with God and the Church.
65745.m: Confession is the sacrament of reconciliation.

65746.q: What is the forgiveness of sins at the end of confession called?
65746.e: The priest gives absolution: ‘I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.’
65746.m: Absolution is the forgiveness of sins.

65747.q: What does the seal of confession forbid a priest to do?
a: Tell anyone what he has heard
65747.e: The seal of confession is strict: a priest must not reveal to anyone what was entrusted to him in confession.
65747.m: The priest must keep to himself what is said in confession.

65748.q: What is the small room or booth where people usually used to go to confession called?
65748.e: In the confessional, the priest and the person confessing are separated by a grille. Today there are also confession rooms for a conversation.
65748.m: Confession used to take place mostly in the confessional.

65749.q: What is honestly thinking about your own wrongdoings before confession called?
65749.e: Before confession, in the examination of conscience, you think about where you have done wrong to others, to yourself or to God.
65749.m: Before confession you examine your conscience.

65750.q: According to Church law, how often should Catholics go to confession at least?
65750.e: Since the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, there has been a duty to go to confession at least once a year, usually before Easter.
65750.m: Catholics should go to confession at least once a year.

65751.q: According to Catholic teaching, what belongs to confession apart from confessing and absolution?
65751.e: Confession includes remorse, confessing your sins, penance or making amends, and absolution.
65751.m: Without remorse there is no valid confession.

65752.q: Who may give absolution in the Catholic Church?
65752.e: Only ordained priests and bishops may give absolution in the sacrament of penance.
65752.m: Only a priest or bishop gives absolution.

65753.q: What does the Latin word ‘confirmatio’, from which ‘confirmation’ comes, mean?
65753.e: Confirmatio means strengthening or affirming: confirmation strengthens the faith that was given at baptism.

65754.q: Who usually gives the sacrament of confirmation?
a: The bishop or someone he appoints
65754.e: The ordinary minister of confirmation is the bishop. He can appoint a priest, such as an episcopal vicar, to do it.
65754.m: Confirmation is usually given by the bishop.

65755.q: Which oil is used to anoint the forehead at confirmation?
65755.e: Chrism is a blessed oil made of olive oil and balsam. With it, the minister makes a cross on the forehead.
65755.m: At confirmation the forehead is anointed with chrism.

65756.q: Which event in the Bible is confirmation especially linked to?
65756.e: At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down on the disciples. According to Catholic belief, confirmation also gives the Holy Spirit.
65756.m: Confirmation recalls the events of Pentecost.

65757.q: How many ‘gifts of the Holy Spirit’ are traditionally named at confirmation?
65757.e: The seven gifts are wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord.
65757.m: Tradition names seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

65758.q: What is the ceremony in Protestant churches called at which young people confirm their baptism?
65758.e: In Reformed and Lutheran churches, young people affirm their own yes to their baptism at confirmation.

65759.q: What words does the bishop say when anointing at confirmation?
a: ‘Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.’
‘I baptise you in the name of the Father.’
65759.e: With these words the minister makes the sign of the cross with chrism on the forehead of the person being confirmed.
65759.m: The words of confirmation are ‘Be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit.’

65760.q: Who accompanies a young person being confirmed as a special companion?
65760.e: The confirmation sponsor accompanies the young person on their path of faith and places a hand on their shoulder during the ceremony.
65760.m: A sponsor accompanies the person being confirmed.

65761.q: What was the anointing of the sick usually called in the past?
65761.e: Because for a long time it was mainly given to the dying, it was called extreme unction. The Second Vatican Council stressed the name anointing of the sick.
65761.m: What used to be extreme unction is now called anointing of the sick.

65762.q: What does the priest anoint with in the anointing of the sick?
65762.e: The priest uses the oil of the sick blessed by the bishop. The Letter of James already says that the sick should be anointed with oil.
